summary: Describes using Hierarchical Host Identity Tags as self-asserting IPv6 addresses to serve as trustable identifiers for drones in Unmanned Aircraft System Remote ID. In this role they are called DRIP Entity Tags. It updates RFC 7401 and another related RFC.

eli5.summary: Every drone gets a special ID tag that proves who it is and tells where to look it up, a bit like a license plate that is hard to fake.

subtitle: Self-asserting IPv6 addresses that give every drone a hard-to-fake ID and a pointer to its registry.

tldr.problem: Drone Remote ID needs an identifier that is unique, hard to spoof, tells observers which registry lists it, and fits in 19 characters.
tldr.mechanism: Hierarchical Host Identity Tags (HHITs) put a 28-bit registry hierarchy and an 8-bit suite ID next to a 64-bit hash of the drone's public key, forming a 128-bit IPv6 address. When used for drones they are called DRIP Entity Tags (DETs).
tldr.outcome: A DET is only trustable together with registration and proof of key ownership. The RFC says plainly that the 64-bit hash is small enough that registration is a MUST.

today: RFC 9374 is a Proposed Standard from March 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 7343 and RFC 7401.

sections.title: Why Drones Need a Self-Asserting ID
sections.content:
The Drone Remote ID Protocol (DRIP) requirements in RFC 9153 ask for a UAS Remote ID that is unique, non-spoofable, tied to a registry, and fits within a 19-character identifier. This RFC is a foundational DRIP document. It uses Hierarchical Host Identity Tags (HHITs) as self-asserting IPv6 addresses. Within Remote ID they are called DRIP Entity Tags (DETs): HHIT is used for the technology and DET for the UAS context.

HHITs are valid but non-routable IPv6 addresses. They extend the Host Identity Tags of RFC 7401 with an explicit hierarchy, so the registry that holds a tag can be found, for example through DNS, and a third party can endorse the identity.

The RFC contrasts this with UUIDs or serial numbers used as a certificate subject. In that case there is no unique proof of ownership or registration, and the same Remote ID could appear in several certificate authorities. A HHIT cannot be in more than one registry within a registry system. A tag that cannot be looked up or validated is either fraudulent or revoked or expired.
sections.eli5: A normal name tag can be copied by anyone. This ID is made from a secret only the drone knows, and it says which office keeps the record.

sections.title: The HHIT Format and Its Hierarchy
sections.content:
A HHIT is a 128-bit value built from four parts: an IPv6 prefix (up to 28 bits), a 28-bit Hierarchy ID (HID), an 8-bit HHIT Suite ID, and an ORCHID hash filling the rest. With a 28-bit prefix the hash is 64 bits, compared with 96 bits in a standard HIT.

The HID has two 14-bit halves. The Registered Assigning Authority (RAA) manages a registry of HDAs; for example a national civil aviation authority could be one. The HHIT Domain Authority (HDA) is assigned by an RAA and may be an Internet service provider, a UAS Service Supplier (USS) or another third party that manages UAS services. Each field allows 16,384 values.

The prefix for DETs is 2001:30::/28. It MUST be distinct from the flat HIT prefix, because otherwise the first 4 bits of the RAA would be read as the HIT Suite ID. The Suite ID names the algorithms: the initial list has 0 reserved, 1, 2 and 3 taken from RFC 7401, and 5 for EdDSA/cSHAKE128. Values 254 and 255 are HDA private use.

An RAA MUST provide services to allocate HDAs and, at minimum, MUST maintain a DNS zone for HDA zone delegation. An HDA must maintain public and private UAS registration information.
sections.eli5: Think of a phone number: a country part, a city part, then your own number. The drone ID has a registry part, a company part, and a fingerprint-like part that only fits its own key.

sections.title: EdDSA and the ORCHID Hash
sections.content:
The RFC adds the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA, RFC 8032) as a Host Identity algorithm with HI Algorithm value 13. The defined curves are EdDSA25519 (1, RECOMMENDED), EdDSA25519ph (2), EdDSA448 (3, RECOMMENDED) and EdDSA448ph (4), with 0 reserved. This changes some HIP parameters, but they should not be needed in a DRIP implementation that does not use HIP.

The hash is built with an improved ORCHID construction based on RFC 7343. The new form is Prefix | Info | OGA ID | Hash, and the total MUST be 128 bits. Unlike the older ORCHIDv2, the prefix, the extra information (the HID) and the suite ID are all fed into the hash, so they cannot be swapped without detection. The hash uses cSHAKE128, a variable-output function, called as cSHAKE128(Input, L, "", Context ID) where the input is the prefix, additional information, OGA ID and HOST_ID.

The Context ID for HHITs is 0x00B5 A69C 795D F5D5 F008 7F56 843F 2C40. For backward compatibility, the RFC also describes how to encode and decode ORCHIDs for HIPv2 with prefix 2001:20::/28 and a 96-bit hash.
sections.eli5: The tag is a scrambled fingerprint of the drone's public key, and the registry part is scrambled in too. Change any part and the fingerprint no longer matches.

sections.title: HHITs as DRIP Entity Tags
sections.content:
DETs use the EdDSA/cSHAKE128 suite. The ASTM Remote ID standard carries them in a UAS ID of type 4, the Specific Session ID. The first byte of the 20-byte UAS ID holds the SSI type, leaving at most 19 bytes. SSI type 1 is the IETF DRIP entity ID.

A HI and its DET SHOULD NOT be transferable between aircraft or replacement electronics, and the private key SHOULD be held in a cryptographically secure component. DETs are registered with HDAs, and the registration process is what ensures global uniqueness.

An 88-byte self-proof (timestamps, HHIT and signature) lets an observer confirm Remote ID ownership. For observers without Internet access, a 200-byte offline self-endorsement carries the HDA's signature over the aircraft's HHIT. The strongest proof arises when the observer also sees the aircraft at the location claimed in a hashed location message.

Where only a serial number fits, the RFC defines a Base32 encoding of the low-order 72 bits (suite ID plus hash), left-padded with 3 zero bits, into the 15-character manufacturer serial field of CTA 2063-A. A trusted mapping service from the manufacturer code to the prefix and HID is then needed.
sections.eli5: The drone shouts its tag. An observer can ask the registry about it, or check a signed note the drone carries, and then see with their own eyes that the drone is where it says.

sections.title: Finding a DET Through DNS
sections.content:
The RFC gives two example ways to store DETs in DNS and does not recommend one. One uses fully qualified names such as 20010030.hhit.arpa.. The other uses reverse lookups as IPv6 addresses. An FQDN built from the RAA and HDA values can point to the USS that holds the public and private information for the aircraft, for example 100.50.20010030.hhit.arpa..

The HDA SHOULD provide DNS service for its zone. The DNS entry can also act as a revocation service by returning a record showing the HI was revoked instead of returning the HI. Detailed guidance is left to the DRIP registration document.
sections.eli5: DNS works like a phone book. You look up the tag and find the office that knows who owns the drone.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated 2001:30::/28 in the IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry for DETs (allocation date 2022-12). It also created a Drone Remote ID Protocol registry with two subregistries: HHIT Prefixes (new entries by Expert Review) and HHIT Suite IDs (new entries by IETF Review). Values 1 to 31 are reserved for IDs that MUST be replicated as HIT Suite IDs, and 32 to 255 are for those that need not be.

The Context ID is registered in the CGA Extension Type Tags registry. In the HIP Parameters registry, the RFC adds the EdDSA Host ID (13), a new EdDSA Curve Label subregistry, and the HIT Suite ID EdDSA/cSHAKE128 (5).
sections.eli5: The special address block and the new ID numbers are written in the official lists so nobody else reuses them.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
The 64-bit hash is a real risk for second pre-image attacks. Producing 2^64 EdDSA keypairs is economically feasible, and an attacker who only needs to steal any one of 1,024 aircraft faces what amounts to a 54-bit condition. For this reason HHIT registration is a MUST and observers SHOULD validate the registration through registry lookups or broadcast proofs. Registries block takeover but not impersonation, which can be mitigated by using DNS (with DNSSEC recommended) to fetch the HI.

The Basic ID Message that carries the DET is too small for proof of ownership. Only the Authentication Message can carry it, and even that does not prove which aircraft sent it, so full trust needs a visual sighting or validated location. On collisions, the RFC gives a 0.01% chance in a population of 66 million and 1% at 663 million, and registries MUST reject a collision.

There is no expectation of privacy for DETs. They are broadcast in the clear over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and changing the DET alone does not stop tracking because MAC addresses and other identifiers also link operations. Post-quantum cryptography is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The ID is short, so a determined cheater could try to make a fake that looks the same. That is why a drone must also be signed up with a registry, and why anyone nearby can read its tag.
